subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Weather and Sensor Limits
description: A fast breakdown of Weather and Sensor Limits for builders.

hook.text: Most self-driving testing happens in sunny cities like Phoenix—but most of the world isn't Phoenix.

buildup.text: Heavy rain scatters lidar pulses, snow covers lane markings, and fog blinds cameras.

discovery.text: Even a thin layer of dirt on a sensor can cause the car to misread its surroundings completely.

twist.text: Self-driving companies quietly avoid launching in cities with harsh winters for exactly this reason.

climax.text: Solving weather is not optional—half the world's roads face conditions that break current sensor systems.

punchline.text: Self-driving works great until the weather disagrees.

quiz.question: Why do self-driving companies mostly test in sunny cities?
options: Sensors work best in clear conditions

details.summary: Heavy rain, snow, fog, and ice degrade the performance of all autonomous vehicle sensors, creating conditions where even the most advanced self-driving systems may need to slow down, limit features, or stop.
details.whyItMatters: Weather remains one of the biggest unsolved challenges for autonomous driving. A system that only works in fair weather cannot replace human drivers in climates where bad weather is common.
takeaways: Rain and snow scatter lidar laser pulses and obscure cameras
Ice and snow can cover lane markings and road edges
Most AV services currently restrict operations in severe weather

faq.question: Can any self-driving car operate safely in heavy snow?
faq.answer: Not reliably yet. Snow covers lane markings, road edges, and signs that AV systems depend on. It also degrades lidar and camera performance. Several companies are developing snow-specific perception models but widespread capability is years away.

faq.question: How do AV companies handle weather limitations today?
faq.answer: Most restrict or suspend autonomous operations when weather exceeds sensor capabilities. Waymo reduces its operating area during heavy rain. This limitation is acceptable for initial deployment but must be solved for broad adoption.
